meaning: She of the ointment jar (Egyptian bꜣstt)

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bone'.
Short rounded vowel in the first syllable.
Glottal stop [ʔ], the Egyptological alef (ꜣ, U+A723) that Allen reconstructs before the stressed syllable in the earliest form.
Short close front vowel in the stressed syllable.
Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], as in English 'see'.
Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the second -t marks the feminine suffix and was usually not pronounced in speech.

pronunciation.approximation: 'boo-ISS-tee' — say 'boo', then a tiny catch before 'iss', ending with 'tee' (the final t is often silent).

kin.label: Greek

kin.label: Earlier Egyptian
kin.form: Bast / Bꜣst, the shorter Old Kingdom form (Faulkner, s.v. bꜣstt)

pronunciation.note: Allen (The Ancient Egyptian Language: A Historical Study, 2013, p. 74) reconstructs the earliest form as buʔístit or buʔístiat; by the first millennium the name had become *Ubaste and then Coptic ⲟⲩⲃⲁⲥⲧⲉ (Oubaste) /ʔuˈβastə/. The meaning of the name remains uncertain; the lexicon glosses it 'She of the ointment jar'. The final -t is a feminine marker often silent in speech, and the ꜣ represents a glottal stop. PUNICODEX uses the registrable alef ꜣ (U+A723); the double -tt- is orthographic. This is a Tier 1 restoration — the alef is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. Sources: Allen 2013, p. 74; Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. bꜣstt; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache III, s.v. bꜣstt; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), for the phonological background of Egyptian alef and feminine -t.

domains.title: Goddess of the Hearth and the Claw
domains.subtitle: Cats, Childbirth, and Domestic Sanctity
domains.lead: Bꜣstt begins as a lioness and ends as a cat. In the Old Kingdom she is a fierce daughter of Re, one of the raging eyes of the sun; by the Late Period she has become the benevolent lady of the home, her round face and upright ears copied by millions of household cats. The transformation is not a decline but an expansion: she learns to keep watch at the cradle as well as at the battlefield — and to receive her pilgrims with music and wine.

cards.name: The Cat
cards.desc: Bastet's later animal form; the cat protects the home from vermin and evil, and embodies solar warmth.

cards.name: The Lioness
cards.desc: Her older, fiercer aspect as a daughter of Re who fights the chaos serpent Apep.

cards.name: Music and Ecstasy
cards.desc: Her festivals featured sistrums, drums, and dancing; she is a goddess of controlled revelry.

cards.name: Guardian of the Home
cards.desc: Amulets of Bastet protected women in childbirth and children against malign forces.

mythology.lead: Bastet's myths are fewer and more fragmented than those of Isis or Horus — Egypt never wrote her a great cycle — but what survives is vivid: the wandering solar eye that must be talked home, the red beer that ends a massacre, and the festival that Herodotus judged the merriest in Egypt.

myths.title: The Lioness Talked Home
myths.text: In the theology of the solar eye, the goddess who is Re's own eye grows angry and abandons Egypt for the Nubian desert, taking leonine form; the sun dims and the land withers behind her. The gods send the eloquent Thoth — disguised, in the Late Ptolemaic Papyrus Jumilhac, as a baboon — to coax her back with a flood of words and stories. When the eye returns she comes home in gentler form: the cat, Bastet, the pacified one, and the homecoming itself becomes festival. The same pattern, without her name, underlies the Book of the Heavenly Cow, where the eye must be retrieved before creation itself can be repaired. The Jumilhac account is late — a mythological manual of the Ptolemaic age — but the grammar it preserves is old: wrath departs south, eloquence retrieves it, and the returning goddess is gentler than the one who left. The myth reads Bastet's two bodies, lioness and cat, as a single biography — ferocity that has been talked home, and asked to stay.

myths.title: Red Beer on the Field of Slaughter
myths.text: When humanity plots against the aging Re, the sun-god sends his eye against them, and the eye — a lioness whom later tradition variously names Sekhmet or Bastet — falls upon mankind in a slaughter so complete that even the gods grow afraid the earth will be emptied. In the version painted on the royal tomb walls of the Book of the Heavenly Cow — Seti I (KV17), Ramesses VI (KV9), and the gilded shrines of Tutankhamun (KV62) — Re halts the carnage with a stratagem: the gods brew seven thousand jars of beer, dye them red with ochre, and flood the fields until the land lies red as blood. The eye, sworn to drink only blood, drinks, wakes drunk, wakes changed — and the text itself renames her Hathor, the rejoicing one, while her wrath keeps the name Sekhmet. The festival of drunkenness at Thebes kept this transformation liturgically alive. The myth's theology is precise and unnerving: divine violence is never defeated, only inebriated into harmlessness — and then commemorated, every year, with a hangover.

myths.title: Seven Hundred Thousand Pilgrims
myths.text: The fullest account of Bastet's worship was written by a Greek tourist. Herodotus (Histories 2.59–60) describes her annual festival at Boubastis as the most joyous in Egypt: some seven hundred thousand pilgrims — he says this without counting children — sailed the canals in crowded boats, men and women together, clapping castanets, shaking rattles, and playing flutes, while on the banks the townsfolk jeered at them with obscene gestures that the boaters cheerfully answered in kind. At the city they made great sacrifices — Herodotus remarks that more wine was drunk at this festival than in all the rest of Egypt's year — and the household cats of the honoured dead were mummified and carried to sacred ground at Bubastis (2.66–67). He also judged the temple of Bastet the loveliest in Egypt, with its grove of trees, its spring, and its lake (2.137–138). The historian's disapproval of animal veneration never quite hides his astonishment. What his account preserves is a goddess whose cult was defined by collective, licensed joy — religion as festival rather than fear — and an Egypt that laughed all the way upriver to her door.

myths.title: The Cat at the Prow
myths.text: Book of the Dead spell 17 preserves one of Egypt's strangest divine self-declarations: 'I am the cat beside whom the ished-tree was split, on the night when the enemies of the lord of all were destroyed.' The cat is the sun-god's own fighting form — the Great Cat, the text's glosses explain, a form of Re — who guards the solar barque through the underworld hours and beheads the chaos serpent at Heliopolis. Later tradition read Bastet herself into the passage, and the identification gave the house-cat a cosmic job description: the same animal that keeps granaries free of vermin keeps the universe free of Apep. Spell 17 is deliberately cryptic — a commentary text whose glosses multiply identities — and the cat passage sits among identifications of the deceased with Re, Atum, and Osiris, so the claim belongs to the whole company of the justified. But its instinct is Bastet's own: the watchful eye that never sleeps, small enough for a windowsill, large enough for the sky. The domestic and the cosmic are, for this goddess, the same work at different scales.

myths.title: Artemis of the Egyptians
myths.text: When Herodotus came to Bubastis in the fifth century BCE he needed a Greek face for the lioness-cat of Egypt, and he chose Artemis: he calls her temple 'the temple of Artemis' in Greek translation, and later Greek writers repeat the equation as if it were obvious. The resemblance is thin — Artemis the virgin huntress shares little theology with Bastet — but the comparison fixes something real: both goddesses hold the wild at the boundary of the city, tamed enough to protect, fierce enough to terrify. In Roman times the equation softened further; her name survived less in cult than in the calendar, in the Coptic month that kept her sound. What the Greek translation cannot carry is the domestic heart of Bastet: a goddess whose temple was praised as the most beautiful in Egypt, whose pilgrims drank the year's largest ration of wine, and whose cat guarded not the hunt but the house. The equation says more about Greek habits of translation than about the goddess herself — and what it mistranslated was her tenderness.

lore.syncretism: Bastet overlaps with Sekhmet as the pacified form of the solar eye; one text's destroyer is another's house-cat. She was also identified with Hathor in her musical and erotic aspects, and with Isis as protector of the child Horus. Greeks equated her with Artemis, another virgin huntress with a fierce streak, and sometimes with Aphrodite because of her festivals' sexual license. In Roman Egypt her cult spread alongside that of Isis, and her cat iconography influenced medieval European images of the cat as both demonic and protective. The Coptic name Oubaste preserves her sound long after her temples closed.
lore.culturalLegacy: Bastet is the ancestor of every famous cat. Her image underlies the seated feline statuette, the 'cat lady' archetype, and the double reputation of cats as guardians and familiars; medieval Europe, forgetting her temples, made the cat ambiguous — demonic in one legend, protective in the next — precisely the double nature Bastet had refined two thousand years earlier. Modern Kemetic and Neopagan practice invokes her for home protection, fertility, and pleasure; her name brands cat sanctuaries, museum exhibitions, and a small industry of bronze reproductions. The excavations at Tell Basta continue to yield her votive cats and jewelry, studied as evidence of the ancient animal-cult economy and of some of history's earliest pet-keeping. Bastet endures because her theology never needed rescuing from metaphor: the divine can sit on a windowsill, purring, and still be a daughter of the sun.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Bastet is the goddess of thresholds. She lives where the wild presses against the wall of the house: the cat who sleeps on the bed but still dreams of the hunt. Her mythology is the domestication of solar power — not its weakening, but its decision to protect something small.

There is a wisdom in her later form that the earlier lioness could not teach. To guard a child, to keep watch through the night, to turn a corner of the home into a sanctuary — these are not lesser magics than tearing apart chaos. They are the magics that make chaos worth defeating. Bastet asks us to honor the fierce thing that has chosen to be gentle, and to remember that the claw and the purr belong to the same creature.

lore.archaeology: The temple of Bastet at Tell Basta (Per-Bastet/Boubastis) has yielded statues, jewelry, and one of the largest animal cemeteries in Egypt: hundreds of thousands of mummified cats deposited as votives from the Late Period into Roman times. Bronze cat statuettes, often inlaid with gold earrings, are common in museum collections; examples come from Saqqara, Thebes, and Tanis. Reliefs in the Valley of the Kings show Bastet as a daughter of Re in the solar barque, and the temple foundations Herodotus praised (Histories 2.137–138) have been partially excavated at the modern tell.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written b-ꜣ-s-t-t, often with an ointment-jar determinative (V30) that gives rise to the gloss 'she of the ointment jar.' Allen reconstructs an early pronunciation close to buʔístit, with a glottal stop represented by the alef ꜣ (U+A723). The doubled t is orthographic; the final consonant is a feminine marker often silent in speech. Coptic writes ⲟⲩⲃⲁⲥⲧⲉ (Oubaste). The meaning of the root remains uncertain, and PuniCodex preserves the historic spelling Bꜣstt as a Tier 1 restoration that signals the alef — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses — and the feminine ending.
